header.scope: Lost: international business moved to local acquiring; US stayed with us
header.tag_why: The new head of payments compared approval performance by country, card type and issuer, using Adyen's country-level test on his own traffic, against our average uplift deck. The champion who bought us had left, and we never met his replacement before renewal.

messaging_changes.current_line: Customers see an average uplift in authorization rates with Authorization Boost and Adaptive Acceptance.
messaging_changes.change: For payments leaders, replace the average-uplift line with an account-specific one: 'Your approval rate in each market, by card type and issuer, and what we'd fix.' Say 'approvals', not 'authorization' or 'uplift'. Back it with an analysis of their own traffic, not the Authorization Boost average.
messaging_changes.why: We led with the average uplift. The buyer rejected it out loud ('that's an average. What's mine?') and said 'I can't take an average to my CFO'. He was asking about approvals by country, card type and issuer.

messaging_changes.change: For renewing accounts where a new payments leader has taken over, open with a per-market review of their own approvals and declines before they run one themselves. Frame it as 'money left on the table' in their markets, list the specific issues we would fix, and deliver it fast, before any competitor test finishes.
messaging_changes.why: The new head of payments started by pulling declines by country. Our analysis was called 'the most useful thing we'd sent him', but it landed three weeks after he asked, when the competitor's test had already finished.

messaging_changes.change: Add a proof point to the support story for payments leaders: a named person at Stripe who reviews their approvals every month, by market, and brings them what to fix. Keep this separate from the response-time tiers.
messaging_changes.why: The buyer asked who at Stripe looks at his numbers every month and the rep had no name. What he wanted was a market-by-market view of his own approval rates, with reasons.

messaging_changes.change: Instruction for marketing (no copy until the answer is confirmed): write a direct answer to 'why not local acquiring?' for international markets, and decide whether we can offer a test on the prospect's own international traffic with results reported by country.
messaging_changes.why: The competitor won by testing on the buyer's own traffic and reporting results by country, and the buyer had adopted the 'Local cards, local rails' frame. Our rep had no answer to 'local acquiring'.

On our last call the recommendation had already gone to the CFO two weeks earlier. The transcript does not show that anyone from our side ever spoke to the CFO.

competitor.insight: Adyen didn't win with a claim. They won by running a test on his own traffic and reporting results by country. After that, Stefan asked us questions at the level of country, card type and issuer, and we answered with an average. We don't know the test results, and the rep had no answer to local acquiring at all, so whether we can compete on it is an open positioning question, not a settled one.
competitor.messaging: Offer a proof-on-your-traffic option for international markets and publish a clear answer to the question 'why not local acquiring?'

message.insight: M4's average uplift was rejected out loud. M6's independent ROI study has the same flaw: it is somebody else's number. The one thing that got a positive reaction was the customer-specific analysis, and it arrived too late to matter. The rep's view that we weren't really pitching because it was a renewal is the problem itself: a new decider meant this was a new sale. Developer love and working billing (M2, M7) kept the US but did not hold international.
message.messaging: Rewrite M4 from 'average uplift' to 'your approval rate by market, and what we'd fix', backed by an account-level analysis.

decided.insight: The rep says nothing could have been done, but her own account describes a window. Stefan asked for his numbers. Our analysis found fixable issues and was called the most useful thing we'd sent. It arrived three weeks later, after Adyen's test had finished. We first learned of the evaluation when Stefan asked to split the contract, so the loss came from being late and unaware, not from a deal that was unwinnable.
decided.messaging: Make a fast turnaround on account-specific approval analysis part of the promise to at-risk and renewing accounts.

gaps.insight: The gap was not capability. We could produce the analysis, just not on demand. The bigger gap was a named owner reviewing his numbers every month. M5's tiered response times answer a support question, but he asked for proactive ownership of performance. He declined the roadmap session because he wanted his current numbers, not future features.
gaps.messaging: Add a named performance contact with a monthly approval review to the support story, not just response-time tiers.

language.insight: He frames the problem as lost money in specific markets and says 'approvals'. We say 'authorization' and 'uplift', which sounds like product vocabulary. 'Local cards, local rails' shows he had already adopted the competitor's frame. His remark about hearing from Stripe only when he said he was leaving points to a reactive-vendor perception, but the transcript doesn't establish which company or situation he meant.
language.messaging: Use 'approvals' and 'money left on the table in your markets' in place of 'authorization uplift' when talking to payments leaders.

close.rep_takeaway: When the person who bought us leaves, treat the renewal as a new sale. Find and meet the new owner, and bring them their own numbers before they ask for them. Healthy growth with no tickets told us nothing about a head of payments pulling declines by country. The analysis that impressed Stefan existed; it just arrived after the decision.
